attachments.origin_landmark: humeral head: lateral epicondyle; ulnar head: posterior ulna

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population (2 heads sharing one belly)
functional_compartments.function_note: Runs in its own fibro-osseous groove on the distal ulna, stabilized by a subsheath of the extensor retinaculum -- a common site of tendinopathy/subluxation ('ECU snapping') in racquet sports.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Probe placed longitudinally (long axis) over the most ulnar of the extensor-mass muscle bellies on the dorsomedial forearm, localized by palpation distal to the lateral epicondyle/olecranon while the patient performs resisted wrist extension combined with ulnar deviation.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Superficial extensor compartment, most ulnar of the common-extensor-origin muscles, running distally in its own groove on the ulnar head/distal ulna.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Contracts selectively with resisted wrist extension plus ulnar deviation (distinguishing it from ECRL/ECRB, which deviate radially); tracks the ulnar border of the forearm down to its groove on the distal ulna.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: One of four muscles injected under ultrasound guidance (10-30 U incobotulinumtoxinA/muscle, split site if muscle bulk requires it) in a clinical series treating chronic lateral epicondylitis; injections were placed at the muscle's motor end plate region under long-axis probe view, localized first by palpation from the epicondyle during resisted contraction. This is a pain/overuse-treatment context rather than post-stroke spasticity, but the sonographic localization technique is the same. ECU was the least frequently symptomatic of the four muscles in that series (29.2% of patients).
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Galvan Ruiz A, Vergara Diaz G, Rendon Fernandez B, Echevarria Ruiz de Vargas C, 'Effects of Ultrasound-Guided Administration of Botulinum Toxin (IncobotulinumtoxinA) in Patients with Lateral Epicondylitis', Toxins 11(1):46 (2019), doi:10.3390/toxins11010046 (https://doi.org/10.3390/toxins11010046) -- retrieved via PubMed

trigger_points.location_description: Belly in the proximal third of the ulnar dorsal forearm.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Ulnar side of the dorsal wrist around the ulnar styloid and 6th extensor compartment, less often the ulnar dorsum of the hand. Travell and Simons regard ECU trigger points as less common than those of the radial extensors.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Repetitive ulnar deviation with extension (hammering, backhand strokes, typing in ulnar deviation), direct blows.
trigger_points.notes: Non-myofascial differential: TFCC tear, DRUJ instability or arthritis, lunotriquetral instability, ulnar impaction, ECU subluxation, dorsal ulnar sensory neuritis, pisotriquetral arthritis (volar), C8 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 34; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 34 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: With FCU it forms the ulnar-deviation couple; with ECRL/ECRB it extends the wrist. Because the tendon runs in a fixed groove on the ulnar head, it acts as a dynamic stabiliser of the DRUJ and ulnar carpus, most important in pronation and during loaded rotation. Its elbow moment is negligible, but its epicondylar origin belongs to the common extensor tendon and its origin is occasionally implicated in lateral epicondylalgia. Repetitive ulnar deviation with pronation (racquet sports, rowing) provokes ECU tendinopathy and subluxation.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None named. Adjacent structures and relations: Anconeus and supinator proximally (Kocher interval between anconeus and ECU), the posterior border of the ulna medially, the ulnar head and DRUJ capsule distally, the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve crossing near its tendon at the wrist.

trigger_points.location: Proximal third of the muscle belly along the dorsal-ulnar forearm, a few centimetres distal to the epicondyle.
trigger_points.referred_pain: the ulnar side of the dorsal wrist over the ulnar styloid and 5th metacarpal base.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Ulnar dorsal wrist pain on gripping with ulnar deviation, painful ECU tendon; mistaken for ECU tendinopathy or subluxation, TFCC tear or ulnar impaction. Entrapment: None. Associated TrPs: ECRB, extensor digitorum, FCU (synergist in ulnar deviation), triceps.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: latissimus dorsi and serratus posterior superior (ulnar forearm and hand)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this territory from elsewhere
clinical.notes: The anconeus–ECU (Kocher) interval is the classic lateral approach to the radial head and lateral ligament complex; the ECU subsheath must be repaired when violated at the wrist. Ulnar deviation on wrist extension is lost in PIN palsy (ECU paralysed, ECRL spared).
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.

tests.name: Chair and coffee-cup tests
tests.performance: Lifting a chair or a full cup with a pronated grip
tests.source: Zwerus EL, Somford MP, Maissan F, Heisen J, Eygendaal D, van den Bekerom MPJ. Physical examination of the elbow, what is the evidence? A systematic literature review. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(19):1253–1260.

clinical.tests_caveat: Values are taken from the cited primary studies. Most series are small and reference standards differ (surgery, arthroscopy, electrodiagnostics), so treat the numbers as indicative. The systematic review of Zwerus et al. (2018) found 24 described elbow tests, only 14 with any accuracy data, and concluded that no single test can rule an elbow diagnosis in or out on its own. Where no accuracy data exist, this is stated rather than estimated.

clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Ulnar deviation: moment arm about 26 mm, the largest deviation moment arm of any wrist motor [10, 12]. Extension: Small and forearm-position-dependent: about 0.9 mm in pronation, 7–8 mm in neutral and supination. In the pronated working position it is therefore almost a pure ulnar deviator; in supination it becomes an extensor–ulnar deviator [12]. PCSA about 2.5 cm², equal to ECRB [8, 12]. Balance role: Its principal normal role is to oppose the radial-deviating moments of ECRL and ECRB, keeping the 3rd metacarpal aligned with the radius; loss of ECU (PIN palsy) produces radial deviation of the wrist [12]. Distal radioulnar joint: Dynamic stabilizer of the DRUJ (with pronator quadratus); tensions the dorsal TFCC through its subsheath [37, 38]. Carpal stability: Carpal pronator: isolated loading pronates both carpal rows and widens the scapholunate interval in every forearm position, so isolated ECU strengthening is avoided in scapholunate rehabilitation [14, 16, 17].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: 6th compartment synovial sheath inside the subsheath; no bursa. Coupled structures: Ulnar head and DRUJ, TFCC, ulnocarpal ligaments, 5th carpometacarpal joint, dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve (crosses the tendon), FCU (ulnar deviation couple) [37–39].

trigger_points.location: Belly in the proximal third of the ulnar dorsal forearm [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Ulnar side of the dorsal wrist around the ulnar styloid and 6th compartment, less often the ulnar dorsum of the hand [2, 3]. Travell and Simons regard ECU trigger points as less common than those of the radial extensors.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Repetitive ulnar deviation with extension (hammering, backhand strokes, typing in ulnar deviation), direct blows [2, 3].

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into ECU territory (ulnar dorsal wrist)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: TFCC tear, DRUJ instability or arthritis, lunotriquetral instability, ulnar impaction, ECU subluxation, dorsal ulnar sensory neuritis, pisotriquetral arthritis (volar), C8 radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: ECU tendinopathy and tenosynovitis are common causes of ulnar-sided wrist pain in racquet sports and golf. Subsheath rupture allows subluxation or dislocation of the tendon out of the ulnar groove, classically after forceful supination with palmar flexion and ulnar deviation (two-handed backhand); the tendon then snaps with forearm rotation [39]. ECU pathology coexists with TFCC tears, DRUJ and lunotriquetral instability [39]. In rheumatoid caput ulnae the tendon migrates volarly and becomes a flexor–ulnar deviator; in spastic wrists distension of the sheath allows the same volar-ulnar migration, converting the ECU into a weak wrist flexor and aggravating the flexion deformity, which is why ECU is transferred to ECRB [12].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
